Reading 1 · Andrew: When Gaming Took Over

A1–A2 short interview · about 200 words · based only on the interview provided
WARM-UPCan video games become a problem? Why?

Andrew started playing video games at a neighbour's house when he was about nine or ten. When he was around twelve or thirteen, he got an Xbox. His mother tried to limit his gaming to one or two hours a day. At first, Andrew played sports games. Later, he played games such as Call of Duty and Halo.

In his junior year of high school, Andrew moved to California and lost many of his friends. Gaming helped him stay in contact with old friends and also gave him an escape.

In his second semester of college, gaming became a serious problem. Andrew skipped classes and homework and played games all day. He failed all his classes and was dismissed from college. Later, he went to community college, but the same problem happened again. His family tried to talk to him about his gaming several times.

At the age of twenty-two, Andrew stopped gaming completely. About a year later, he felt closer to his family and friends and became more productive. He also found other hobbies, including photography and camping.

Andrew says that many people can manage gaming without a problem, but some people are at risk. He thinks young people should have other hobbies too, and he suggests keeping a game console in a public part of the home instead of simply banning games.

Reading 2 · Short Interview with FabuRocks

A1–A2 adaptation based only on the interview details provided
WARM-UPCan gaming help someone learn or communicate? How?
Hi FabuRocks! Tell us a little about yourself.
I’m 14. I’m a gamer, YouTuber, livestreamer and podcaster. I have .
How did you start creating gaming content?
I started when I was 7. I had problems with speaking, and normal speech therapy did not help me much. My parents saw that gaming and making videos helped me speak more. First, I made YouTube videos. Later, I started livestreaming.
How has gaming changed your life?
It changed my life a lot. Now I speak better, have conversations and can be understood. Creating content has made me more confident.
Why did you become a content creator?
Creating content was a kind of therapy for me. It helped my speech and everyday challenges.
What games do you play?
I am a variety streamer. Many famous gamers focus on one game, but I like playing different games.
What have you learned from streaming?
You need support. Even adult streamers need help from family or friends. My parents helped me a lot.
What do you think about social media?
It is good in moderation, but people can become addicted to it.
What is your main message?
Just be yourself. You do not have to be like everybody else.

Grammar

GRAMMAR · A2 · GAMING STORIES & ADVICE

Grammar for telling stories and giving advice

Practise two grammar patterns that you need for the comic, readings, videos and speaking tasks.

Past Simple · Tell the story

Use Past Simple to tell completed events in the past.

Affirmative: subject + past form → Aidan felt strange.
Negative: didn't + base verb → Andrew didn't go to class.
Question: Did + subject + base verb? → Did Dia call for help?

1. Choose the correct verb form

Choose the correct Past Simple form.

2. Complete the sentence

Write the correct Past Simple form. You can also say the answer.

3. Personal story · Read and retell

Leo's Saturday
Last Saturday, Leo planned to play online for one hour. He started a new game with two friends and soon forgot about the time. After three hours, he felt tired and got a headache. His friend Maya noticed that he was quiet and asked if he was okay. Leo stopped the game, drank some water and went outside with his dog. Later, he came back and finished his homework. He decided that next weekend he would set a timer before he started playing.

Retell Leo's story in your own words. Try to use at least 5 Past Simple verbs. Aim for 30–60 seconds.

Can & Should · Benefits, Problems & Advice

Use can / can't for ability or possible results, and should / shouldn't for advice.

can / can't + base verb → Games can develop problem-solving skills.
should / shouldn't + base verb → Players should take a break.
After these modal verbs, use the base verb: can help, not can helps; should take, not should to take.

1. Choose can, can't, should or shouldn't

Choose the form that best completes the sentence.

2. Correct the mistake

Rewrite the sentence correctly. You can type or say your corrected version.

3. Mini speaking · Problems & Advice

Answer the questions. Try to use can / can't / should / shouldn't several times.

1. What problems can happen if a person plays for too long?
2. What should a player do if they start to lose control of gaming time?
3. What should parents do about loot boxes and in-game purchases?
4. How can games be useful without becoming unhealthy?

Are video games more helpful or harmful?

Question: Do you think video games are more helpful or more harmful for young people? Give your opinion and explain your reasons.

1
Collect ideas

2. Problems

Your notes are saved to the idea bank automatically as you type.

Create your paragraph skeleton
Use the ideas in your bank to plan the structure. Write notes or fragments — not finished sentences yet.
What is your main answer to “Are video games more helpful or harmful for young people?”
Which benefit matters most? Use an idea from Reading, Watching, Speaking or your experience.
Give one specific example: problem-solving, decision-making, confidence, communication or another benefit.
Which problem matters most? Think about addiction, losing control, loot boxes, money or sleep.
Add one concrete example from the lesson or your experience.
What should young people remember? What can or should they do?
3
Write independently
Turn your own skeleton into a 120–150 word paragraph. Aim for about 150 words. No model answer is provided.
Use your own language. Draw on the Comic Strip, Reading, Watching, Vocab, Grammar and your experience, but do not copy a previous text. Use examples and connect your ideas naturally.

GAME · CODENAMES · CO-OP

Code Names · Teacher + Student

Play together against a virtual Opponent. One Game Code connects both screens live.

How to play / Как играть
Very simple rules / Очень простые правила
Teacher = Spymaster I know the secret. Я знаю секрет.
Student = Guesser I guess the words. Я угадываю слова.
Virtual Opponent Computer player. Виртуальный соперник.

🇬🇧 English

1You play together. Teacher knows the secret. Student guesses.
2Teacher opens the key. Only Teacher sees which words are ours, Opponent, Neutral and Danger.
3Teacher gives one clue + a number. Example: school — 2.
4Student guesses. Student clicks a word once. Both screens update automatically.
5Student presses Pass turn once. Then the Virtual Opponent automatically takes one Opponent word.
6Win: find all Our team words first. Lose: click Danger or let the Opponent finish first.

🇷🇺 Русский

1Вы играете вместе. Учитель знает секрет. Ученик угадывает.
2Учитель открывает ключ. Только учитель видит наши слова, Opponent, Neutral и Danger.
3Учитель говорит одно слово + число. Например: school — 2.
4Ученик угадывает. Ученик нажимает слово один раз. Оба экрана обновляются автоматически.
5Ученик нажимает Pass turn один раз. Потом виртуальный соперник автоматически забирает одно своё слово.
6Победа: найдите все наши слова первыми. Поражение: нажать Danger или дать сопернику закончить первым.
